<style>
.shark-guide-wrap {

}

.ocean-hero {

}

}

.hero-shark-art {
  flex: 0 0 230px;
  margin: 0 auto;
  z-index: 2;
  animation: floatShark 4s ease-in-out infinite;
}

@keyframes floatShark {
  0%, 100% { transform: translateY(0px) rotate(-1deg); }
  50% { transform: translateY(-9px) rotate(2deg); }
}

.bubble-dot {
  position: absolute;
  border-radius: 50%;

}

.story-overview-box {

}

}

.tab-cards-grid {

  margin-bottom: 2.4rem;
}

.tab-card {
  background: #ffffff;
  border: 2px solid #e0f2fe;
  border-radius: 18px;
  padding: 1.35rem 1.4rem;
  box-shadow: 0 6px 16px rgba(12, 74, 110, 0.06);

  display: flex;
  flex-direction: column;
  justify-content: space-between;
}

.tab-card:hover {
  transform: translateY(-4px);
  border-color: #38bdf8;
  box-shadow: 0 10px 22px rgba(2, 132, 199, 0.14);
}

.tab-card-header {

    <div class="story-overview-copy">
      <h3>🌊 The Big Question We're Investigating</h3>
      <p style="margin-bottom: 0.5rem;">
        Along Southwest Florida's Gulf coast, microscopic algae called <em>Karenia brevis</em> bloom nearly every year,
        releasing neurotoxins and depleting oxygen in coastal waters. Meanwhile, South Florida's Atlantic coast around Miami
        and Biscayne Bay is usually sheltered—until rare ocean current events (like in <strong>2018</strong>) carry red tide
        right around the Florida Keys!
      </p>
      <p style="margin-bottom: 0;">
        By combining <strong>13 years of University of Miami shark drumline surveys</strong> with <strong>Florida FWC &amp; NOAA
        red tide water monitoring</strong>, this website explores how sharks move between coasts and how their catch rates change during bloom years.
      </p>
    </div>
  </div>
